common_name: Princess Diana Alstroemeria (Dwarf Yellow Peruvian Lily with Red Blotches)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about four to six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Princess Diana is a compact patio-bred selection from the Princess Lily series developed by Royal Van Santen in the Netherlands.

directions: Set out tuberous roots in spring, spreading the brittle fingers shallowly in loose, well-drained soil rather than burying them deep, since Princess Lily selections form a shallower, more fibrous root mass than full-size garden Alstroemeria. Princess Diana carries clear yellow flowers heavily blotched in brick-red on the upper petals, held on a naturally low, tidy mound bred specifically for patio pots and small border edges rather than cutting. Deadhead by pulling entire spent stems from the base rather than snipping, which encourages continuous rebloom through summer, and protect containers from hard freezes since dwarf Princess types are less cold-tolerant in pots than in open ground. Where marginally hardy, a heavy winter mulch over the crown helps it return the following spring.

common_name: Princess Louise Alstroemeria (Dwarf Magenta Peruvian Lily with Speckled Throat)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about four to six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Princess Louise is a dwarf, long-blooming selection from the Princess Lily patio series.

directions: Plant tuberous roots shallowly in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates, spacing plants close together for the fullest patio-pot display. Princess Louise opens vivid magenta-pink flowers with a yellow throat flecked in dark maroon streaks, a striking bicolor combination held well above the compact, mounding foliage typical of the dwarf Princess Lily series. Remove spent stems by pulling rather than cutting to trigger fresh flushes of bloom over a long summer season, and feed container plants lightly through the growing period since dwarf types in pots exhaust nutrients faster than those in open beds. In zones at the cold edge of its range, mulch the crown heavily or overwinter potted specimens in an unheated garage.

common_name: Princess Mathilde Alstroemeria (Dwarf Peachy-Orange Peruvian Lily Flecked with Burgundy)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about four to six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Princess Mathilde (PP 20,992) is a patented dwarf selection from the Princess Lily series bred for compact container growth.

directions: Set tuberous roots shallowly in loose, well-drained potting mix or garden soil in full sun, keeping the naturally low, dense habit in mind when choosing container size. Princess Mathilde produces peachy-orange flowers flecked with burgundy streaking on the upper petals, a warm blended color that stands out against its compact, evenly mounded foliage. Pull rather than cut faded flower stems at the base to prompt continuous new bloom through the growing season, and water container plantings more frequently than in-ground plants since dwarf pot culture dries out faster. Because it is a patented selection, propagation is intended for personal garden use rather than commercial division and resale.

common_name: Third Harmonic Alstroemeria (Saffron-Orange Peruvian Lily with Dark Petal Markings)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Third Harmonic is a California hybrid raised by breeder George Hare from a cross of 'Harmony' and Alstroemeria aurantiaca.

directions: Plant tuberous roots about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, handling the brittle roots gently and allowing room for a vigorous, taller-growing clump. Third Harmonic opens in saffron-yellow and peach shades marked with dark stripes near the petal tips, deepening toward orange and red-backed petals as the flowers age, a rich, layered coloring that draws bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Pull spent flowering stems from the base rather than cutting them to encourage repeat bloom over a long season, and divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain vigor. It tends to grow larger and more vigorously than many dwarf patio Alstroemeria, making it better suited to open borders than small containers.

common_name: Star of Holland Amaryllis (Coral-Red Amaryllis with White Eye)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Star of Holland is a long-established Dutch amaryllis cultivar that holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Star of Holland produces broad, brilliant coral-red flowers with a crisp white eye and a pale green throat, a bold, high-contrast pattern combined with a reliable habit of throwing multiple flower stems per bulb over consecutive seasons. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round, naturalizing and increasing into a fuller clump with time. Allow foliage to grow and yellow naturally after flowering rather than cutting it back early, since the leaves recharge the bulb for the following year's bloom, and for indoor forcing plant with about a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix.

common_name: Susan Amaryllis (Pale Rose-Pink Amaryllis with Lime-Green Netted Throat)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Susan is a Dutch-bred amaryllis noted for its flat-faced form and finely netted petal pattern.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Susan bears large, flat-faced blooms brushed in pale rose-pink with a bright lime-green throat ringed by small red dots, the broad, overlapping petals showing a delicate netted veining that distinguishes it from more solid-colored amaryllis cultivars. Each bulb typically sends up several flower stems in succession, extending the display over weeks rather than an single flush. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb, and for winter forcing plant with roughly a third of the bulb above the potting mix in a bright, cool location.

common_name: Lady Jane Amaryllis (Fully Double Apricot-Pink Amaryllis with White Feathering)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Lady Jane belongs to the Double Galaxy Group of amaryllis, bred for its ruffled, lily-like double flowers.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Lady Jane produces fully double, ruffled flowers in soft apricot-pink feathered and striped with white, the many-petaled form giving each bloom a full, lily-like fullness rather than the simple trumpet shape of single-flowered amaryllis cultivars. Each bulb typically sends up two to three stems bearing several blooms apiece, extending the display over a longer period than single-flowered types. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally after flowering to recharge the bulb, and for indoor forcing plant with about a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix in a bright, draft-free spot.
